sentences.text: Appellant is the 2nd respondent in O.P.(MV).No.470 of 2007 filed before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal, Pathanamthitta.
The claim petition was filed by respondents 1 to 5 herein, being the legal representatives of deceased Rajeev Cherian, who died in a motor accident.
The fatal accident occurred on 26.12.2006 at 08:45 pm on the Kulakadu- Thukkalassery road while the motor cycle ridden by Rajeev Cherian capsized and fell into a gutter.
The motor cycle belonged to the 6th respondent herein and was insured with the appellant.

Before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal,
Rs.5,00,250/- was claimed as compensation, against which the Tribunal awarded Rs.4,05,500/-.

The challenge in this appeal is primarily on the ground that, since the accident occurred when 2025:KER:32751 the deceased was riding the motor cycle, he had stepped into the shoes of the owner and cannot therefore be construed as a third party covered by the insurance policy.

2. Heard Senior Advocates George Cherian for the appellant and Mathews Jacob for respondents 1 to 5.
3.
Senior Advocate George Cherian appearing for the appellant submitted that the claim petition is filed under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act and is hence applicable only to third parties.

It is contended that the appellant had specifically contended in the written statement that it had no liability to indemnify the insured, since the deceased was the rider of the vehicle and therefore, not a third party.

It is submitted that the legal position is covered by the decision of the Apex Court in Ningamma and Another v. United India Insurance Company Limited [2009 KHC 5046] and followed by this Court in a series of decisions, including Jiljet and Another v. Stamphen George and Others [2018 (5) KHC 206].
2025:KER:32751 4.

entities.text: Ningamma and Another v. United India Insurance Company Limited [2009 KHC 5046]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Jiljet and Another v. Stamphen George and Others [2018 (5) KHC 206]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In reply, Senior Advocate Mathews Jacob contended that, in so far as the deceased was not the owner of the motor cycle, he should be treated as a third party for the purpose of insurance.
It is argued that the burden was upon the insurer to prove that the deceased had borrowed the vehicle from the owner, and thus, had stepped into the shoes of the owner.
The insurer having failed to discharge the burden, the Tribunal was justified in awarding compensation to the legal heirs.

Reliance is placed on the decision in Kunjila and Others v. Mary and Others [ILR 2024 (2) Kerala 315] to contend that, even if the deceased is taken to have stepped into the shoes of the owner,
respondents 1 to 5 will be entitled for the personal accident coverage for which the owner was entitled.
5.

entities.text: Kunjila and Others v. Mary and Others [ILR 2024 (2) Kerala 315]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: A perusal of the impugned award shows that the appellant had raised a specific contention, citing Ningamma (supra) that, since the deceased was driving the motor cycle after borrowing it from the real owner, he had stepped into the shoes of the owner and hence, his legal heirs cannot claim 2025:KER:32751 compensation under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act.

The Tribunal brushed aside that contention by holding Ningamma to be having no application to the facts of the case, on the premise that the appellant had no case that the deceased had hired the vehicle from the owner.

The said finding of the Tribunal cannot be countenanced in the light of the legal position laid down in Oriental Insurance Company Limited v. Rajni Devi [2008 ACJ 1441(SC)], wherein it is held that Section 163A of the M.V.Act does not have any application in respect of an accident in which the M/S.Icici Lombard General Insurance ... vs Beena Rajeev on 10 April, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/5930196/
3 owner of the motor vehicle himself is involved.

entities.text: Oriental Insurance Company Limited v. Rajni Devi [2008 ACJ 1441(SC)]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: M/S.Icici Lombard General Insurance ... vs Beena Rajeev
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is also held that the liability under Section 163A being on the owner of the vehicle, he cannot be both, claimant as well as recipient.

The legal position is reiterated in Ningamma, the relevant portion of which reads as under;
"19.We
have already extracted Section 163 A of the MVA hereinbefore.
A bare perusal of the said provision would make it explicitly clear that persons like the deceased in the present 2025:KER:32751 case would step into the shoes of the owner of the vehicle.

In a case wherein the victim died or where he was permanently disabled due to an accident arising out of the aforesaid motor vehicle in that event the liability to make payment of the compensation is on the insurance company or the owner, as the case may be as provided under Section 163-A.
But if it is proved that the driver is the owner of the motor vehicle, in that case the owner could not himself be a recipient of compensation as the liability to pay the same is on him.
This proposition is absolutely clear on a reading of Section 163-A of the MVA.
Accordingly, the legal representatives of the deceased who have stepped into the shoes of the owner of the motor vehicle could not have claimed compensation under Section 163-A of the MVA. "

6. Therefore, irrespective of whether the deceased had borrowed the vehicle or not, as he was riding the vehicle at the time of accident, the claim filed by the legal representatives under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act cannot be entertained.

7. The contention based on Kunjila (supra) is also unsustainable, since the subject policy did not provide personal 2025:KER:32751 accident coverage for the owner/driver, whereas, in Kunjila's case, coverage for personal accident was provided in Section 3 among the terms and conditions of that Policy.
For the aforementioned reasons, the appeal is allowed and the impugned award is set aside.
